# Homework Report

I first loaded the Reddit stock sentiment dataset (`load_dataset_1`), containing 847 documents across three sentiment categories: `-1.0` (315), `0.0` (423), and `1.0` (109). I inspected the data using `inspect_data_tool` (`inspect_data_3`) and checked for missing values (`check_missing_4`) and duplicates (`check_duplicates_6`). No missing values were found, but 23 duplicate entries were identified and removed. The resulting dataset contained 813 documents. I then examined document lengths using `describe_data_tool` (`describe_data_7`). The average length was approximately 148 characters, with a median of 80 and a maximum of 2,753. This suggests that most Reddit comments were relatively short, while a few much longer posts increased the average length. The positive sentiment category had the highest average document length (166 characters), although document lengths varied considerably within each category.

![Document length distribution](../plots/韋妍伃_homework_plot_describe_data_7.png)


Next, I constructed a Document-Term Matrix (DTM) using `build_dtm_tool` (`dtm_8`), containing 813 documents and 4,313 unique terms. The matrix had a sparsity of 99.5249%, indicating that most terms appeared in only a small fraction of the documents. Term frequency analysis (`term_freq_9`) showed that common words such as "the" (874), "to" (554), and "and" (471) appeared frequently. The DTM heatmap (`dtm_heatmap_10`) also demonstrated this sparse structure. I initially applied variance filtering with a threshold of 0.1 (`variance_filter_11`), retaining only 45 features. Since this removed most of the vocabulary, I changed the threshold to 0.01 (`variance_filter_12`), which retained 490 features.
I then applied Spearman correlation filtering with a threshold of 0.1, retaining 13 features for category `0.0` (`spearman_filter_17`), 21 for `-1.0` (`spearman_filter_18`), and 39 for `1.0` (`spearman_filter_19`). For the neutral category (`0.0`), selected terms included "year", "trade", "economy", and "trump", suggesting that many distinguishing features were related to general economic or political discussions rather than explicit sentiment. The negative category (`-1.0`) included words such as "trust", "retard", "fucking", and "economy", which may reflect criticism, frustration, or negative expressions. In contrast, the positive category (`1.0`) contained terms such as "nice", "good", "exciting", "potential", "dividends", and "green", suggesting more optimistic or favorable discussions about stocks and technology. However, some words appeared across multiple categories, indicating that individual terms alone may not be sufficient to determine sentiment. I also examined correlations among the 20 highest-variance terms using `feature_correlation_matrix_tool` (`feature_corr_20`) to explore potential redundancy between features.


![DTM heatmap](../plots/韋妍伃_homework_plot_dtm_heatmap_10.png)

![Feature correlation matrix](../plots/韋妍伃_homework_plot_feature_corr_20.png)

For pattern mining, I applied the FP-Growth algorithm with variance-based filtering to all three sentiment categories. Using a minimum support count of 6, I discovered 29 frequent patterns in category `0.0` (`mine_patterns_10`) and 37 patterns in category `-1.0` (`mine_patterns_11`). For example, "deal", "say", and "today" each had a support of 8 in category `0.0`, while "war", "buying", and "trust" each had a support of 8 in category `-1.0`. For category `1.0`, I used a lower minimum support count of 4 (`mine_patterns_13`), which identified 19 patterns, including "doing" (support = 9), "economy" (support = 6), and "nice" (support = 4). These patterns reveal frequently occurring terms within each sentiment group. However, many patterns consisted of general vocabulary rather than clearly sentiment-specific expressions, suggesting that additional preprocessing or more selective feature filtering could improve their interpretability.

I then applied three dimensionality reduction methods to visualize the 813 documents in two dimensions. PCA (`reduce_dims_14`) explained 26.70% of the total variance through the first principal component and 5.12% through the second, giving a combined explained variance of 31.82%. This indicates that the two-dimensional PCA representation captures only part of the variation in the original document features. I also applied t-SNE (`reduce_dims_15`) and UMAP (`reduce_dims_16`) to explore nonlinear relationships between documents. Unlike PCA, these methods are designed to emphasize local neighborhood structure, which can help reveal patterns that may not be visible through linear projection. However, the returned numerical coordinates alone are insufficient to determine whether the three sentiment categories form clearly separated clusters.

![PCA visualization](../plots/韋妍伃_homework_plot_reduce_dims_14.png)

![t-SNE visualization](../plots/韋妍伃_homework_plot_reduce_dims_15.png)

![UMAP visualization](../plots/韋妍伃_homework_plot_reduce_dims_16.png)

Finally, I converted the sentiment labels into one-hot encoded vectors using `binarize_labels_tool` (`binarize_labels_17`) and examined document similarity using cosine similarity. Documents at indices 1 and 2 both belonged to category `0.0`, but their cosine similarity was only 0.2004 (`cosine_sim_18`). In contrast, documents at indices 0 and 3 belonged to different sentiment categories (`-1.0` and `1.0`, respectively) and had a much lower cosine similarity of 0.0585 (`cosine_sim_19`). These comparisons suggest that documents within the same sentiment category do not necessarily share similar vocabulary, while documents from different categories may have even less lexical overlap. However, these two comparisons alone are insufficient to establish a general relationship between sentiment labels and cosine similarity.
